chapters.situation: Gandhi is in Durban, getting to know the Indian community and Dada Abdulla's lawsuit. He has already clashed with a magistrate over his turban.
chapters.summary: Gandhi learns bookkeeping to understand the case and agrees to go to Pretoria, privately hoping to settle it out of court. He refuses to buy a bedding ticket. At Maritzburg a white passenger objects to him, and he is ordered to the van compartment despite his first-class ticket. He refuses, and a constable pushes him off the train. Shivering all night in the waiting room, he decides not to run home but to fight the 'deep disease of colour prejudice'.

updates.gandhi: Thrown off the train at Pietermaritzburg for being 'coloured'. Spends a freezing night and resolves to stay and fight colour prejudice, seeking redress only so far as it helps remove the prejudice.
updates.abdulla: Trusts Gandhi after a week. Warns him to buy a bedding ticket. After the incident he complains to the railway and wires merchants along the route to look after him.
updates.tyeb: The opposing party in the lawsuit; Gandhi hopes to befriend him and settle.
updates.pietermaritzburg: Where Gandhi is pushed off the train in the bitter cold, the defining night of his South African life.
updates.racism: Thrown out of first class for his colour. Gandhi sees the insult as 'only a symptom of the deep disease of colour prejudice'.
updates.compromise: Even before arriving, Gandhi wants to settle the lawsuit out of court.

status.gandhi: On the way to Pretoria after the Maritzburg night

chapters.situation: Thrown off the train at Pietermaritzburg, Gandhi has resolved to continue to Pretoria and fight colour prejudice.
chapters.summary: On the stagecoach from Charlestown, the white coach leader seats Gandhi outside. When ordered to sit on a dirty sack at his feet, Gandhi refuses, and the man beats him while he clings to the rail until passengers intervene. In Johannesburg a hotel turns him away. Abdul Gani tells him the country is not for men like him. Gandhi gets a first-class ticket to Pretoria from a sympathetic Dutch stationmaster, and an English passenger defends his right to stay in the compartment.

updates.gandhi: Beaten by the coach leader for refusing to sit at his feet, but does not prosecute. Talks his way into first class by appearing in faultless English dress.
updates.abdulgani: Welcomes Gandhi, laughs at his attempt to get a hotel room, and explains that Indians in the Transvaal pocket insults to make money.
updates.transvaal: Indians are refused first-class tickets and treated worse than in Natal.
updates.racism: Beaten on the stagecoach; refused at the Grand National Hotel; challenged by the guard on the Pretoria train.
updates.johannesburg: Gandhi is turned away from the Grand National Hotel.

chapters.situation: After a beating on the stagecoach and a refusal at a Johannesburg hotel, Gandhi reaches Pretoria by first class, alone on a Sunday night.
chapters.summary: An African American stranger guides Gandhi to Johnston's Family Hotel, whose owner first offers dinner in his room and then, after asking the guests, welcomes him to the dining room. Attorney A. W. Baker, also a lay preacher, says there is no barrister's work for him, finds him lodging with a baker's wife, and invites him to daily prayer meetings. Gandhi resolves to study Christianity but not to change religion before understanding his own.

updates.gandhi: Settles in Pretoria with a baker's family at 35 shillings a week. Plans an unbiased study of all religions.
updates.johnston: Hesitates over colour, then asks his guests and welcomes Gandhi to the dining room.
updates.baker: Takes Gandhi on as an informant on the case, finds him lodgings, and starts trying to bring him to Christianity.
updates.christianity: Baker invites Gandhi to daily prayers. Gandhi decides to study Christianity but not to convert before he understands Hinduism.
updates.transvaal: Gandhi arrives in Pretoria, where finding lodgings is hard for 'such as you'.

status.gandhi: In Pretoria, working on Dada Abdulla's case

chapters.situation: Settled in Pretoria with a baker's family, Gandhi starts attending Baker's daily one o'clock prayer meeting.
chapters.summary: Gandhi meets Miss Harris, Miss Gabb and the Quaker Coates, who loads him with Christian books such as Butler's 'Analogy' that leave him unmoved. Coates wants to break his Tulsi-bead necklace, but Gandhi keeps it as a gift from his mother. A Plymouth Brother tells him faith in Jesus frees one from the burden of sin. Gandhi answers that he seeks redemption from sin itself, not from its consequences.

updates.gandhi: Prays with the Christians, keeps a weekly religious diary, and refuses to give up his mother's necklace.
updates.coates: Becomes a close friend. Gives Gandhi many books and asks to break the necklace, believing Gandhi can only be saved through Jesus.
updates.harrisgabb: Host Gandhi to tea every Sunday and tell him of the peace they have found.
updates.plymouth: Argues that believers are freed from sin's burden. Gandhi notices he knowingly sins without concern.
updates.putlibai: The Tulsi-bead necklace she gave her son stays round his neck.
updates.christianity: Gandhi rejects atonement as a release from responsibility: 'I seek to be redeemed from sin itself'. His real difficulty is with the Bible and its accepted interpretation.

chapters.situation: In Pretoria Gandhi divides his time between the lawsuit and long talks with Christian friends.
chapters.summary: Gandhi calls a meeting of Pretoria's Indians, mostly Meman merchants, and gives his first real public speech, on truthfulness in business, sanitation and unity across religion and region. He proposes an association, teaches English to a barber, a clerk and a shopkeeper, and meets the British Agent. He gets the railway to issue first- and second-class tickets to 'properly dressed' Indians, and studies the condition of Indians in the Transvaal and Orange Free State.

updates.gandhi: Gives his first public speech and teaches English to three men. Is starting to organize the community without realizing it.
updates.tyeb: Agrees to help Gandhi reach and study every Indian in Pretoria.
updates.dewet: Sympathetic to Indians but powerless. Shows Gandhi official papers on their treatment.
updates.shyness: Gandhi's first successful speech is in Pretoria, on truth in business.
updates.indians_sa: Gandhi urges Indians to drop distinctions of religion and region and to improve their sanitation.
updates.publicwork: Gandhi holds regular meetings, proposes an association and corresponds with the railway, his first organizing work in South Africa.
updates.truth: His first speech argues that truth is possible, and more necessary, in business.

chapters.situation: Gandhi is studying the legal position of Indians in the Transvaal and the Orange Free State.
chapters.summary: The Orange Free State has expelled Indian traders. The Transvaal charges a £3 poll tax, bars Indians from owning land outside 'locations', and forbids them to use footpaths or go out after 9 p.m. without a pass. The State Attorney, Dr. Krause, a fellow member of Gandhi's Inn, gives him a letter exempting him. A Boer policeman outside President Kruger's house kicks Gandhi off the footpath. Coates offers to be a witness, but Gandhi declines to go to court over a personal grievance.

updates.gandhi: Kicked into the street by a sentry outside Kruger's house. Forgives the man and refuses to sue over a personal grievance.
updates.coates: Takes Gandhi for night walks and witnesses the assault. Offers to testify and reprimands the policeman.
updates.krause: Gives Gandhi a letter allowing him out at any hour and becomes a friend.
updates.kruger: His modest house on President Street is guarded by the sentry who kicks Gandhi.
updates.racism: The £3 poll tax, the 9 p.m. curfew, and footpath bans enforced by kicks.
updates.ahimsa: Gandhi refuses to go to law over personal injuries; the man is only following the system.
updates.transvaal: Asiatics' laws: no franchise, no land ownership, segregated 'locations'.

chapters.situation: Having seen the laws against Indians first-hand, Gandhi turns back to his main job, Dada Abdulla's £40,000 lawsuit.
chapters.summary: Gandhi masters the accounts and correspondence and learns that 'facts are three-fourths of the law'. Seeing the costly lawsuit ruining both relatives, he persuades Tyeb Sheth to go to arbitration. Dada Abdulla wins, then agrees to let Tyeb pay about £37,000 in instalments so he avoids bankruptcy. Gandhi concludes that a lawyer's true function is to unite divided parties.

updates.gandhi: Brings the big case to arbitration and an instalment settlement. Learns 'the true practice of law' and the confidence that he can succeed as a lawyer.
updates.abdulla: Wins the arbitration and generously allows his relative Tyeb to pay in instalments over a long period.
updates.tyeb: Agrees to arbitration on Gandhi's advice, loses, and is allowed to pay in instalments rather than face bankruptcy.
updates.pincutt: His maxim that facts are three-fourths of the law proves true.
updates.leonard: Later tells Gandhi: take care of the facts and the law will take care of itself.
updates.compromise: Gandhi's first great settlement. He goes on to spend much of his 20-year practice arranging private compromises.
updates.law: Gandhi finds his vocation in mastering facts and reconciling parties.
updates.truth: 'Facts mean truth, and once we adhere to truth, the law comes to our aid naturally.'

chapters.situation: With the lawsuit settled, Gandhi's year in Pretoria has also been a year of intense religious discussion with Christian friends who hope he will convert.
chapters.summary: Baker takes Gandhi to the Wellington Convention, a Christian revival, enduring colour-bar problems on the way. Gandhi admires the devotion but cannot accept Jesus as the only son of God, atonement through his blood, or Christianity as the greatest religion. He is equally troubled by Hinduism's untouchability and sects. Raychandbhai counsels patience. Gandhi reads the Koran, corresponds with Edward Maitland, and is overwhelmed by Tolstoy's 'The Kingdom of God Is Within You'.

updates.gandhi: Rejects conversion but is equally critical of Hinduism. Studies the Koran, Maitland and Tolstoy. His religious quest becomes a living force.
updates.baker: Takes Gandhi to the Wellington Convention and stands up for him at a hotel, hoping prayer will win him over.
updates.murray: Chairs the Wellington Convention; Gandhi meets him.
updates.raychand: By letter, urges patience and deeper study of Hinduism, which he calls unsurpassed in depth.
updates.maitland: Corresponds with Gandhi and sends 'The Perfect Way' and 'The New Interpretation of the Bible', which seem to support Hinduism.
updates.tolstoy: 'The Kingdom of God Is Within You' overwhelms Gandhi and makes Coates's books 'pale into insignificance'.
updates.abdulla: Keeps urging Gandhi to study Islam.
updates.christianity: Gandhi accepts Jesus as martyr and teacher but not as the only incarnation of God, and cannot see Christianity as the perfect religion.
updates.islam: Gandhi reads Sale's Koran and other books on Islam.
updates.religion: Gandhi critiques Hinduism too: untouchability is 'a rotten part', and he questions why only the Vedas should count as inspired.
updates.untouchability: Gandhi calls untouchability a rotten part or excrescence of Hinduism.

chapters.situation: With the case settled, Gandhi returns to Durban to sail home after his year abroad.
chapters.summary: At his farewell party Gandhi notices a newspaper item about a bill to strip Indians in Natal of the vote. Abdulla Sheth admits the merchants know nothing of politics and have no contact with Christian Indians born in Natal. The guests beg Gandhi to stay a month and lead the fight. He agrees, refusing any fee for public work, and the farewell party becomes a working committee.

updates.gandhi: Cancels his passage and stays a month to fight the Franchise Bill, without fees. 'Thus God laid the foundations of my life in South Africa.'
updates.abdulla: Explains the community's political ignorance and asks how Gandhi will be paid; Gandhi refuses fees for public work.
updates.escombe: Had earlier encouraged Indians to register as voters, to help in his own election.
updates.franchise: The Natal Franchise Bill would remove Indians' right to vote. Gandhi calls it 'the first nail into our coffin'.
updates.indians_sa: Christian Indians born in Natal are cut off from the merchants; Gandhi resolves to claim them as part of the community.
updates.publicwork: The farewell party becomes a working committee.

status.gandhi: Staying in Natal to fight the Franchise Bill

chapters.situation: Gandhi has agreed to stay a month to fight the bill disenfranchising Natal's Indians.
chapters.summary: Under Haji Muhammad's presidency, merchants, clerks and Christian youths of every religion and region volunteer together. They win a two-day delay and present an overnight petition, but the bill passes. A petition with 10,000 signatures goes to Lord Ripon, and The Times of India and the London Times support it. Asked to stay permanently, Gandhi refuses a salary for public work; about twenty merchants give him a year's legal retainers instead. He settles in Natal.

updates.gandhi: Organizes petitions to the Natal legislature and Lord Ripon. Agrees to settle in Natal on legal retainers, with no pay for public work.
updates.hajimuhammad: Presides over the meeting that resolves to fight the Franchise Bill.
updates.abdulla: His house becomes a public office. He buys furniture for Gandhi's new household instead of a farewell purse.
updates.paul: Brings Christian Indian youths in as volunteers.
updates.godfrey: Helps bring Christian Indian youths in as volunteers.
updates.rustomji: One of the top signature-gatherers for the Ripon petition.
updates.dawud: Drives around all day collecting signatures.
updates.escombe: Sent a telegram asking for the bill's discussion to be postponed.
updates.ripon: Receives a 10,000-signature petition against the Franchise Bill.
updates.franchise: The bill passes the Natal Assembly despite the petition. The fight moves to London, with hope of a veto.
updates.indians_sa: All distinctions of class, religion and region are forgotten: the community feels 'one and indivisible'.
updates.publicwork: Gandhi accepts no salary for public work, in order to keep his independence and the community's commitment.

status.gandhi: Settled in Natal as a lawyer and community leader, 1894

chapters.situation: Gandhi has decided to settle in Natal as a lawyer for Indian merchants while leading the community's public work.
chapters.summary: Gandhi applies to be admitted as an advocate of Natal's Supreme Court. The Law Society opposes him, ostensibly over his missing original certificate but in truth because he is not white. The court rejects the objection, saying the law makes no distinction of colour, and admits him. When the Chief Justice orders him to remove his turban, he complies, saving his strength for 'bigger battles', to his friends' dismay. He reflects that insistence on truth taught him the value of compromise.

updates.gandhi: Admitted as an advocate of the Natal Supreme Court over the Law Society's objection. Removes his turban in court, choosing his battles.
updates.escombe: As Attorney General, presents Gandhi's application for admission without fee.
updates.abdulla: Swears an affidavit for Gandhi; disapproves of his giving up the turban.
updates.racism: The Law Society argues that coloured men could not have been intended to join the bar; the Supreme Court disagrees.
updates.compromise: 'Truth is hard as adamant and tender as a blossom.' Knowing when to yield becomes part of satyagraha.
updates.law: Gandhi is admitted to the Natal bar.

status.gandhi: Advocate of the Natal Supreme Court
